meaning: Shows that an action is completely finished, or that something unwanted or irreversible happened, with a tone of regret or frustration.
connection: Verb te-form + しまう (casual: 〜ちゃう／〜じゃう)

senses.label: Finish completely
senses.meaning: The action is done completely, all the way through, like “finish off” or “... up”. Often used with 「全部」, 「もう」, or 「早く」. The volitional 「〜てしまおう」 means “let's just get it all done”.
senses.connection: Volitional verb te-form + しまう／しまった／しまおう
examples: I finished all my homework.
Let's get this job done today.
I ate the whole cake by myself.

senses.label: Regret / something unexpected
senses.meaning: Something the speaker didn't want, and can't undo, has happened. It carries regret or frustration, like “accidentally ...” or “ended up ...”. Usually in the past: 「〜てしまった」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + しまった (with non-volitional verbs like 「忘れる」, 「壊れる」, 「遅れる」, it almost always has this meaning)
examples: I left my umbrella on the train.
I'm sorry I was late for our appointment.
I broke a precious plate.

notes: Casual contractions: てしまう→ちゃう, でしまう→じゃう; てしまった→ちゃった／じゃった.
「ちゃう／じゃう」 are casual. In formal writing or with superiors, use 「〜てしまう」.
With volitional verbs, either meaning is possible. Context decides.

daily.title: Confessing to a friend
daily.description: When admitting you couldn't resist something, casual 「ちゃった」 sounds natural.
daily.example: I ate cake again.

daily.title: Doing chores on the weekend
daily.description: The volitional 「〜てしまおう」 is for getting the rest done in one go.
daily.example: Let's get the cleaning done this morning.

daily.title: Upset after losing something
daily.description: 「〜てしまった」 expresses regret over a loss.
daily.example: I lost my wallet.

work.title: Apologizing to a client or boss
work.description: When your mistake causes trouble, apologize formally with 「〜てしまい、申し訳ありません」.
work.example: I apologize for the delay in getting back to you.

work.title: Finishing work before leaving
work.description: Telling coworkers you'll finish what you're working on first.
work.example: I'll just finish putting this document together.

etymology: 「しまう」 is written 「仕舞う」 in kanji. Its original meaning is “to finish, to wrap up; to put away”. It shares a root with 「おしまい」 (“the end”). From “wrapping something up” it came to mean “doing something completely”, and then took on a tone of regret that “it can't be undone”. The casual 「ちゃう」 comes from the sound change 「てしまう→ちまう→ちゃう」.

similar.title: 〜ておく
similar.explanation: Both can mean "get something done", but 〜ておく focuses on preparing in advance for later, while 〜てしまう focuses on finishing it off or on regret. 「ビールを冷やしておく」 is chilling beer ahead of a party; 「ビールを全部飲んでしまった」 is having drunk it all (possibly with regret).

similar.title: 〜終わる
similar.explanation: Verb masu-stem + 終わる simply states that an action ends in time (読み終わる = finish reading), with no regret or remorse, and it can't follow non-volitional verbs. 〜てしまう can carry the speaker's subjective evaluation.

similar.title: 〜ている
similar.explanation: 〜てしまっている expresses "a state of having (undesirably) already been completed continues", as in 「もう出発してしまっている」. Plain 〜ている only expresses progress or a resulting state, without the sense of completeness or regret.

meaning: Doing something in advance to prepare for the future, or deliberately leaving something as it is. It can also mean “do it for now”.
connection: Verb te-form + おく (casual: 〜とく／〜どく)

senses.label: Preparing in advance
senses.meaning: Getting something done ahead of time for a later purpose, like “do ... beforehand”. This is the most common use. It often goes with 「前に」, 「までに」, or 「あらかじめ」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + おく／おきます／おいてください
examples: I booked the hotel before the trip.
Please make copies of the materials by tomorrow.
Let's buy the drinks before the party.

senses.label: Leaving as is
senses.meaning: Deliberately keeping a state as it is, without changing it, like “leave it ...”. It is intentional and carries no criticism.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + おく (often 「〜ておいてください」 or 「〜ておいていい」)
examples: You can leave the window open.
Please put it back where it was after you use it.

senses.label: For now
senses.meaning: “I'll just do this for now and deal with the rest later.” A light tone, often used to say what you'll do.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + おく (often with 「とりあえず」 or 「一応」)
examples: For now, I'll just write my name.
I'll check with the teacher, just in case.

notes: Casual contractions: ておく→とく, でおく→どく; ておいて→といて, ておいた→といた. For example, 「買っとく」 and 「読んどいて」.
Use 「〜ておいてください」 to ask someone else. Say 「〜ておきます」 about yourself; it sounds proactive and thoughtful.
As an auxiliary verb, it is usually written in kana as 「おく」, not 「置く」.

daily.title: Getting ready for a party at home
daily.description: Preparing before friends arrive. Casual speech uses 「〜とく」.
daily.example: I'll put the beer in the fridge.

daily.title: Before a trip
daily.description: Booking tickets or hotels in advance with 「〜ておく」.
daily.example: I already bought the shinkansen tickets.

daily.title: A word from family
daily.description: Telling someone to leave something as it is.
daily.example: It's fine to leave the AC on.

work.title: A boss assigns a task
work.description: Asking for preparation before a meeting with 「〜ておいてください」.
work.example: Please read the materials before the meeting.

work.title: Reassuring a client
work.description: 「〜ておきます」 shows you'll take care of it ahead of time.
work.example: Then I'll go ahead and book a meeting room.

etymology: 「おく」 is written 「置く」 in kanji and originally means “to put, to set down”. Putting something somewhere and leaving it there came to mean “keeping a state for later use”. This gave rise to two uses: “preparing in advance” and “leaving as is”. In speech, the vowels in te-o run together and the o drops out, giving 「〜とく」.

similar.title: 〜てある
similar.explanation: 〜てある describes "the state left after someone did something for a purpose", focusing on the resulting state, and the subject is often marked with が (「ビールが冷やしてある」); 〜ておく focuses on the act of preparing itself (「ビールを冷やしておく」).

similar.title: 〜てしまう
similar.explanation: 〜てしまう stresses finishing off or regret; 〜ておく stresses preparing for later. 「食べておく」 is eating something now so you won't be hungry later; 「食べてしまう」 is eating it all up.

similar.title: 〜っぱなし
similar.explanation: 〜っぱなし means "leaving something in a state without dealing with it", with a critical nuance (「電気をつけっぱなしにする」); the "leave as is" of 〜ておく is usually intentional and not critical.

meaning: Trying something to see how it turns out: “try ...ing”, “... and see”.
connection: Verb te-form + みる

senses.label: Try doing
senses.meaning: Doing something to see what happens. It's like “try it and see” in English, where “see” is also part of the idea.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + みる／みた／みます
examples: Let's look up words we don't know in the dictionary.
I tried writing a letter in Japanese.
May I try on these shoes?

senses.label: Want to try
senses.meaning: 「〜てみたい」 means you'd like to give something a try, usually something new to you. It sounds lighter and softer than plain 「〜たい」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + みたい(です)
examples: I'd like to visit Hokkaido someday.
Someday I'd like to try wearing a kimono.

senses.label: Suggestions and invitations
senses.meaning: 「〜てみてください」 and 「〜てみませんか」 encourage someone to give it a try. Softer than a direct order or invitation.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + みてください／みませんか／みたら？
examples: Please try this on.
Why don't we give it a try together?

senses.label: Tried it and found
senses.meaning: 「〜てみたら」 and 「〜てみると」 are followed by a surprise discovery or result: “When I tried ..., it turned out ...”.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + みたら／みると + what you found
examples: I tried the new restaurant, and it was really good.
When I actually tried it, it was surprisingly easy.

notes: As an auxiliary verb, it is usually written in kana as 「みる」. Written 「見る」, it usually means literally “to look”.
Don't confuse it with 「〜てみせる」, which means “to show someone how” or “to make sure you do it”.

daily.title: Trying on clothes in a shop
daily.description: Asking a clerk if you can try something on.
daily.example: May I try this on?

daily.title: Talking about travel dreams with a friend
daily.description: Naming a place you want to experience.
daily.example: I'd love to swim in the sea in Okinawa.

daily.title: Sharing a cooking experience
daily.description: Explaining what you found after trying.
daily.example: I tried making Japanese food, and it was easier than I expected.

work.title: Proposing a new method to your boss
work.description: 「〜てみてはいかがでしょうか」 makes a polite suggestion.
work.example: Why don't we try a new approach?

work.title: A teacher encouraging students
work.description: Having students try on their own first.
work.example: First, try thinking about it yourself.

etymology: 「みる」 is simply 「見る」 (to look, to see). “Do it and then see the result”: the meaning “see” weakened into “try”. English shows a similar idea in phrases like “try it and see” or “have a go and see”.

similar.title: 〜ようとする
similar.explanation: 〜ようとする means "attempt to, be about to"; the action often isn't realized or doesn't succeed (「ドアを開けようとしたが、開かなかった」). 〜てみる means you actually did it to see the result.

similar.title: 〜てみせる
similar.explanation: 〜てみせる means "show someone by doing" or "(be determined to) definitely do" (「必ず合格してみせる」); it has nothing to do with trying.

similar.title: 〜たい
similar.explanation: 〜たい simply means wanting to do something; 〜てみたい means "want to give it a try", usually about something new you haven't done before, and sounds lighter and softer.

meaning: Someone did something on purpose, and the result is still there. It often implies it was done for a reason.
connection: Transitive verb te-form + ある

senses.label: Deliberate resulting state
senses.meaning: Describes a state you can see and implies someone did it on purpose: “has been ...ed”. The doer is usually not mentioned, and the object often takes 「が」.
senses.connection: Noun が + transitive verb te-form + ある (「書く」, 「貼る」, 「置く」, 「飾る」, 「並べる」, etc.)
examples: Today's schedule is written on the blackboard.
There's a calendar on the wall.
Old books are lined up on the bookshelf.

senses.label: Already prepared
senses.meaning: Stresses that something was done in advance for a purpose and is now ready: “already ...”. It's often the result of 「〜ておく」. Here 「を」 can also be kept.
senses.connection: Noun を／が + transitive verb te-form + ある (often with 「もう」)
examples: The hotel's already booked, so don't worry.
There was beer chilling in the fridge.

notes: As a rule it follows transitive verbs. For the resulting state of intransitive verbs, use 「〜ている」 (窓が開いている).
The negative is usually 「〜ていない」 or 「〜てない」, not 「〜てあらない」.

daily.title: Describing a room
daily.description: Showing a guest how the room is decorated.
daily.example: There are flowers on the table.

daily.title: Confirming travel plans
daily.description: Telling family the tickets are taken care of.
daily.example: I already bought the tickets, so we're fine.

daily.title: Reading a sign
daily.description: Saying what is written on a notice or sign.
daily.example: It says “No Smoking” here.

work.title: Reporting to your boss
work.description: Saying that everything for the meeting is ready.
work.example: The meeting materials are already prepared.

work.title: Saying where documents are
work.description: Telling a coworker where something is.
work.example: The documents are on the desk.

etymology: 「ある」 is 「有る／在る」, which expresses the existence of inanimate things. “The result of an action exists there”, so “transitive verb te-form + ある” shows that a deliberate result remains. Classical Japanese already had 「〜てあり」, and the perfective auxiliary 「たり」 itself comes from the fusion of 「て＋あり」.

similar.title: 〜ている
similar.explanation: Intransitive verb + ている only describes a state (「窓が開いている」 = the window is open, regardless of why); transitive verb + てある implies someone did it on purpose (「窓が開けてある」 = someone deliberately opened the window).

similar.title: 〜ておく
similar.explanation: 〜ておく focuses on the act of preparing in advance; 〜てある focuses on the state after the preparation is done. 「予約しておく」→「予約してある」.

meaning: A change in ability, habit, or situation: from not being able to being able, or from not doing to starting to do.
connection: Verb dictionary form / potential form / nai-form + ようになる

senses.label: Becoming able to
senses.meaning: With potential verbs, it shows gaining an ability: “now I can ...”. Usually in the past 「〜ようになった」, since the change has happened.
senses.connection: Potential verb (話せる, 読める, 泳げる, etc.) + ようになる
examples: I practiced every day, and now I can play the piano.
With glasses, I can see the writing on the blackboard clearly.
I want to be able to speak Japanese soon.

senses.label: Change of habit
senses.meaning: With regular verbs, it shows a change in behavior or habit: “have started to ...”. It can also describe changes in society.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ようになる
examples: Since coming to Japan, I've started eating sashimi.
Lately, I've started shopping on my phone.

senses.label: No longer ...
senses.meaning: With the nai-form, it means “no longer ...”. However, 「〜なくなる」 is more natural; 「〜ないようになる」 sounds a bit stiff.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ようになる (more common: 〜なくなる)
examples: The baby has stopped crying at night.

notes: Changes in nouns and adjectives don't use this pattern. Say 「先生になる」 or 「暑くなる」.
「ように」 without 「なる」 may be purpose (忘れないようにメモする) or comparison, which are different grammar points.

daily.title: Talking about your progress
daily.description: Telling a friend how your Japanese has improved.
daily.example: I can understand the news in Japanese now.

daily.title: Talking about a child growing up
daily.description: A parent describes a new skill.
daily.example: My daughter can dress herself now.

daily.title: Talking about habits
daily.description: Describing a change after moving somewhere new.
daily.example: I've started jogging every morning.

work.title: A new employee settling in
work.description: Reporting progress at work to a boss.
work.example: I can finally work on my own now.

work.title: Introducing a new system
work.description: Explaining what becomes possible after an update.
work.example: Starting next month, you'll be able to apply online.

etymology: 「よう」 is written 「様」 in kanji, originally meaning “appearance, state”. 「に」 marks the result of a change, and 「なる」 means “to become”. Literally, it means “to become the state of ...”. When 「様」 is used as a formal noun, it is usually written in kana.

similar.title: 〜ようにする
similar.explanation: 〜ようにする expresses the subject's conscious effort (「毎日運動するようにしている」); 〜ようになる expresses a change that happens naturally as a result.

similar.title: 〜ことになる
similar.explanation: 〜ことになる expresses an arrangement or decision (not made by oneself) (「転勤することになった」); it has nothing to do with gradual changes in ability or habit.

similar.title: 〜くなる／〜になる
similar.explanation: Changes in adjectives and nouns use 高くなる, 静かになる, 医者になる; only changes in verbs use 〜ようになる.

meaning: Making a conscious effort to do (or not do) something. 「〜ようにしている」 describes a habit you keep up.
connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + ようにする

senses.label: Making an effort
senses.meaning: A resolution to be careful to do or not do something from now on: “try to ...”, “make sure to ...”. The point is the effort, not necessarily 100% success.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + ようにする／ようにします
examples: Starting tomorrow, I'll try to get up earlier.
Let's try not to look at our phones before bed.

senses.label: Ongoing habit
senses.meaning: 「〜ようにしている」 is a habit you have formed and keep up: “I make a point of ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + ようにしている
examples: For my health, I make a point of walking every day.
I make sure to eat vegetables every day.

senses.label: Polite request
senses.meaning: 「〜ようにしてください」 asks others to make sure they do something. It is softer than 「〜てください」 and stresses “please be careful to ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + ようにしてください
examples: Please make sure you aren't late for class.
Please be sure to come at eight tomorrow.

notes: The subject must be a person acting on purpose. It can also follow potential verbs, meaning “make it possible to ...” (見えるようにする).
The 「ように」 in 「このようにして」 means “in this way”. It isn't this grammar point.

daily.title: Talking about healthy habits
daily.description: Explaining your lifestyle to a friend.
daily.example: I try not to eat much at night.

daily.title: Reflecting on yourself
daily.description: Making a resolution after a mistake.
daily.example: From now on, I'll try to go to bed earlier.

daily.title: A parent warning a child
daily.description: Reminding a child to be careful.
daily.example: Make sure you don't play in the street.

work.title: A boss reminding staff
work.description: Reminding everyone to be on time before a meeting.
work.example: Please make sure you're not late for the meeting.

work.title: Reassuring a client after a mistake
work.description: Promising to be more careful in the future.
work.example: We will make sure that this kind of mistake does not happen again.

etymology: 「よう（様）」 means “appearance, state”, and 「にする」 means “to make into”. Literally, “to make (your behavior) into the state of ...”. From this came the meaning “to make an effort to do, to be careful to do”.

similar.title: 〜ようになる
similar.explanation: 〜ようになる is a natural change; 〜ようにする is a deliberate effort. 「話せるようになった」 means your ability improved; 「話すようにしている」 means you keep making a point of speaking.

similar.title: 〜ことにする
similar.explanation: 〜ことにする expresses a one-time decision (「タバコをやめることにした」); 〜ようにする expresses ongoing effort and care, not necessarily achieved 100%.

similar.title: 〜ように (purpose)
similar.explanation: In 「忘れないようにメモする」, ように expresses purpose and is followed by another action; in 〜ようにする, ように and する form a single unit.

meaning: The speaker thinks something is possible but isn't sure: “maybe”, “might”.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + かもしれない; na-adjective stem / noun + かもしれない (no 「だ」)

senses.label: Possibility
senses.meaning: Something may be true, with about 50% certainty or less: “maybe”, “might”. Often paired with 「もしかしたら」 or 「ひょっとすると」.
senses.connection: Plain form + かもしれない／かもしれません; past guess: 〜たかもしれない
examples: It might rain in the afternoon.
He may have already gone home.
That person might be a teacher, you know.

senses.label: Softening an opinion
senses.meaning: Makes your opinion sound less certain, and therefore gentler. Often it is really a polite “no” or a suggestion.
senses.connection: Plain form + かもしれません (often with 「ちょっと」 or 「少し」)
examples: That plan might be a bit difficult.
This color might be better.

senses.label: Casual 「かも」
senses.meaning: In casual speech it is often shortened to 「〜かも」. Relaxed, mostly between friends.
senses.connection: Plain form + かも (at the end; 「ね」 or 「よ」 can follow)
examples: This cake might be a little too sweet.
It might rain tomorrow.

notes: Nouns and na-adjectives take no 「だ」: 雨かもしれない (✕雨だかもしれない).
Degree of certainty: 〜に違いない ＞ 〜はずだ ＞ 〜だろう ＞ 〜かもしれない.

daily.title: Checking the weather before going out
daily.description: Reminding family to take an umbrella.
daily.example: It might rain, so let's take an umbrella.

daily.title: A casual guess with friends
daily.description: Guessing who someone is when you see them.
daily.example: That guy might be a teacher.

daily.title: Might be late for a date
daily.description: Letting someone know in advance you may be late.
daily.example: I might be a little late.

work.title: Gently rejecting a proposal
work.description: Politely voicing doubts about a coworker's idea in a meeting.
work.example: That schedule might be a little unrealistic.

work.title: Flagging a risk
work.description: Reporting a possible problem to your boss.
work.example: We might not make the delivery deadline.

etymology: It is made of the question particle 「か」 + the particle 「も」 + 「知れない」 (“cannot be known”). Literally, “whether it is ... or not cannot be known”, hence “maybe”. Today it is usually written in kana. The casual short form 「〜かも」 became widespread in the last few decades.

similar.title: 〜はずだ
similar.explanation: 〜はずだ is a fairly confident judgment based on reasoning or facts ("it should be ..."); 〜かもしれない has low certainty and only says the possibility exists.

similar.title: 〜だろう／〜でしょう
similar.explanation: 〜だろう expresses a fairly confident guess (70-80%); 〜かもしれない is much less certain, meaning only "that can't be ruled out".

similar.title: 〜に違いない
similar.explanation: 〜に違いない expresses strong conviction ("it must be ..."), far more certain than 〜かもしれない.

meaning: A confident conclusion based on evidence or logic (“should be ...”). It can also mean “was supposed to ...” or “no wonder ...”.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + はずだ; na-adjective + な + はずだ; noun + の + はずだ

senses.label: Should be (by logic)
senses.meaning: A fairly confident conclusion based on facts or evidence: “should”, “ought to”. There must be grounds for it, often given with 「〜から」 or 「〜ので」.
senses.connection: Plain form + はずだ／はずです (noun + の, na-adjective + な)
examples: I sent the package yesterday, so it should arrive today.
He lived in Japan for ten years, so his Japanese must be good.
It's Sunday, so the bank should be closed.

senses.label: Was supposed to
senses.meaning: 「〜はずだった」 means something should have happened but didn't. It carries surprise or disappointment and is often followed by 「のに」.
senses.connection: Plain form + はずだった／はずでした (often followed by 「のに」 or 「が」)
examples: The train was supposed to arrive at 9, but it still hasn't come.
Today was supposed to be my day off, but some work suddenly came up.

senses.label: No wonder
senses.meaning: Once you learn the cause, the result suddenly makes sense: “no wonder ...”. Often with 「道理で」 or 「なるほど」.
senses.connection: (Cause) + plain form of the result + はずだ
examples: The AC isn't on. No wonder it's hot.
So he pulled an all-nighter yesterday. No wonder he's sleepy.

notes: There are two negative conclusions: 「〜ないはずだ」 (it shouldn't be) and 「〜はずがない」 (it can't be). The second is much stronger.
It can't express your own will or plans: ✕「明日行くはずです」. Say 「行くつもりです／行く予定です」 instead.

daily.title: Waiting for a delivery
daily.description: Estimating arrival from the shipping date.
daily.example: I sent it yesterday, so it should get there by tomorrow.

daily.title: Can't find something
daily.description: Remembering where you put it.
daily.example: I'm sure I put the keys in my bag, but they're not there.

daily.title: A sudden realization
daily.description: Once you know the cause, it all makes sense.
daily.example: The window was open. No wonder it's cold.

work.title: Confirming meeting arrangements
work.description: Concluding someone should know based on the notice sent.
work.example: I emailed the department manager, so he should be aware.

work.title: Explaining a missed plan
work.description: Telling a coworker the original plan didn't work out.
work.example: It was supposed to be done today, but it looks like it'll take until tomorrow.

etymology: 「はず」 is written 「筈」 in kanji. It originally referred to the notch at the end of an arrow that fits onto the bowstring (矢筈). The arrow's notch and the string "naturally have to fit together", which gave rise to the meaning "it stands to reason, it must be so". As a formal noun in modern Japanese it is usually written in kana.

similar.title: 〜はずがない
similar.explanation: 〜はずがない is a strong denial, "there's absolutely no way ...", much stronger than 〜ないはずだ (it shouldn't be ...).

similar.title: 〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: 〜かもしれない only says something is possible, with low certainty; 〜はずだ is based on solid grounds and is highly certain.

similar.title: 〜わけだ
similar.explanation: Both can mean "no wonder", but 〜わけだ focuses on a conclusion following naturally from a premise or explaining a cause, while 〜はずだ focuses on being convinced because it matches expectations.

similar.title: 〜つもりだ
similar.explanation: 〜つもりだ expresses your own plans; 〜はずだ is an inference about objective facts and cannot describe your own plans.

meaning: An impression based on how something looks (“looks ...”). With verbs, it means something is about to happen (“looks like it's going to ...”).
connection: Verb masu-stem + そうだ; i-adjective minus い + そうだ (いい→よさそう, ない→なさそう); na-adjective stem + そうだ

senses.label: Looks ...
senses.meaning: A judgment based on what you see: “looks ...”, “seems ...”. Only for qualities you haven't confirmed. Don't use it for facts obvious at a glance.
senses.connection: i-adjective minus い / na-adjective stem + そうだ (そうな + noun, そうに + verb)
examples: This cake looks delicious.
The kids are playing and look like they're having fun.
He looked down.

senses.label: About to ...
senses.meaning: With verbs, it predicts from signs that something is about to happen: “looks like it's going to ...”, “is about to ...”. Often with 「今にも」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + そうだ (e.g. 降りそう, 落ちそう, 泣きそう)
examples: The sky looks like it's going to rain any minute.
This shirt button is about to come off.

senses.label: Doesn't look likely
senses.meaning: 「〜そうもない」 and 「〜そうにない」 mean it doesn't look like something will happen.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + そうもない／そうにない
examples: It doesn't look like this work will be done today.
The rain doesn't look like it'll stop.

notes: Irregular forms: いい→よさそう, ない→なさそう, 〜くない→〜くなさそう.
Nouns can't attach directly: ✕学生そうだ. Use 「学生みたいだ」 or 「学生らしい」 instead.
Not used for things obvious at a glance, like 「きれい」 or 「赤い」: ✕このりんごは赤そうだ.
Don't confuse it with hearsay 「降るそうだ」. The appearance form attaches to the masu-stem (降りそうだ).

daily.title: At a pastry shop
daily.description: A natural comment on the cakes in the window.
daily.example: Wow, that cake looks so good!

daily.title: Checking on a friend
daily.description: Asking when a friend looks worn out.
daily.example: You look sleepy. Were you up late last night?

daily.title: Looking at the sky before going out
daily.description: Seeing dark clouds and judging it will rain soon.
daily.example: It looks like rain, so let's bring an umbrella.

work.title: Reporting progress
work.description: Estimating whether work will finish on time.
work.example: At this rate, it looks like we'll be done by Friday.

work.title: Reacting to a proposal
work.description: Giving a first impression of an idea in a meeting.
work.example: This project sounds interesting.

etymology: 「そう」 comes from the kanji 「相」 (さう), originally meaning "outward appearance, look" (as in 人相 "physiognomy" and 手相 "palm lines"). From the medieval period onward 「〜さうなり」 was used as an auxiliary of appearance, which later became modern 〜そうだ. It has a different origin from the hearsay 〜そうだ, which is why the two attach differently.

similar.title: 〜そうだ (hearsay)
similar.explanation: The hearsay form follows the plain form: 「雨が降るそうだ」 = I hear it will rain; the appearance form follows the masu-stem: 「雨が降りそうだ」 = it looks like it's going to rain. The hearsay form has no そうな／そうに forms.

similar.title: 〜ようだ／〜みたいだ
similar.explanation: 〜ようだ is a judgment based on all kinds of information (not just visual) and can follow nouns; the appearance 〜そうだ relies more on the immediate visual impression and cannot directly follow nouns.

similar.title: 〜らしい
similar.explanation: 〜らしい mostly judges based on outside information or hearsay, with the speaker keeping some distance; 〜そうだ is the speaker's direct impression from what they see.

meaning: Passes on information heard from others or seen in the media: “I heard that ...”, “apparently ...”.
connection: Plain form of any word + そうだ (noun / na-adjective: 〜だそうだ)

senses.label: I heard / apparently
senses.meaning: Relays information from other people, newspapers, TV, and so on, as is. The speaker is just passing it on and takes no responsibility for it. The tone is neutral. Often paired with 「〜によると」 or 「〜の話では」.
senses.connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + そうだ; noun / na-adjective + だそうだ
examples: According to the weather forecast, it's going to rain tomorrow.
I heard Tanaka-san is getting married next month.
Apparently his father is a doctor.

senses.label: Reporting past events
senses.meaning: It can follow a past form to report something that already happened. 「そうだ」 itself does not change to the past.
senses.connection: Verb / adjective ta-form + そうだ (✕そうだった)
examples: I heard there was an accident near the station yesterday.
Apparently that shop closed last month.

notes: Only forms like 「そうだ／そうです／そうで」 exist. There is no negative or past, and no 「そうな」 or 「そうに」.
Tell it apart from the appearance form by what comes before: 降るそうだ (hearsay) vs. 降りそうだ (appearance); 高いそうだ (hearsay) vs. 高そうだ (appearance).
It can't be used for things you experienced yourself.

daily.title: Passing on the forecast
daily.description: Telling family what you saw before heading out.
daily.example: I saw on the news that it's supposed to snow tonight.

daily.title: Gossiping with friends
daily.description: Repeating news you heard from someone else.
daily.example: I heard Yamada-san is moving next month.

daily.title: Talking about a restaurant
daily.description: Passing on someone else's opinion of a place.
daily.example: I hear that restaurant is really expensive.

work.title: Relaying news from above
work.description: Passing on to coworkers what the department manager said.
work.example: According to the manager, the meeting starts at three.

work.title: Updating your boss about a client
work.description: Reporting news heard from the client.
work.example: I hear they'll be on holiday starting next week.

etymology: The hearsay そうだ is generally thought to come from expressions like 「…と言う相（さう）だ」, meaning "it is said to be the case that ..."; from the Edo period onward it was used in the form 「〜さうだ」 to relay hearsay. Although it is written the same way as the appearance 〜そうだ, the two long ago split into separate auxiliaries, and they attach in completely different ways.

similar.title: 〜そうだ (appearance)
similar.explanation: The appearance form follows the masu-stem / adjective stem and means "looks ..."; the hearsay form follows the plain form and means "I hear ...". 「おいしそうだ」 = looks delicious; 「おいしいそうだ」 = I hear it's delicious.

similar.title: 〜らしい
similar.explanation: 〜らしい can also express hearsay, but it includes some of the speaker's own guesswork and the source is vaguer; 〜そうだ is a more direct, faithful report.

similar.title: 〜って／〜とのことだ
similar.explanation: In speech, 〜って is often used to relay information (「明日休みだって」); 〜とのことだ is a formal, written way of reporting, common in business.

meaning: A guess or hearsay based on what you've heard or seen (“seems ...”). After nouns, it can also mean “typical of ...”.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + らしい; na-adjective stem / noun + らしい (no 「だ」)

senses.label: Guess / hearsay
senses.meaning: A guess based on outside information, such as something you heard or signs you saw: “seems ...”, “I hear ...”. The speaker keeps some distance and doesn't take full responsibility.
senses.connection: Plain form + らしい (nouns and na-adjective stems attach directly); negative goes before it: 〜ないらしい
examples: The road is wet. It seems it rained during the night.
I hear that shop is closing next month.
It seems he quit his job.

senses.label: Typical of ...
senses.meaning: As a suffix after a noun, it means having the typical qualities of that noun: “...-like”, “just like ...”. The negative 「〜らしくない」 means “not like ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + らしい (春らしい, 男らしい, 子どもらしい, 彼女らしい)
examples: It's a warm, spring-like day today.
Saying something like that isn't like her.

notes: It conjugates like an i-adjective: らしかった, らしく, らしくない.
「素晴らしい」, 「新しい」, 「珍しい」, and 「いやらしい」 are independent adjectives, not this grammar point.

daily.title: Guessing from signs
daily.description: Seeing the wet ground and guessing it rained.
daily.example: The ground is wet. Looks like it rained.

daily.title: Catching up on a friend's news
daily.description: Repeating something you heard, without being sure.
daily.example: I heard Sato-san has a girlfriend now.

daily.title: Commenting on the weather
daily.description: Remarking on how seasonal the weather feels.
daily.example: It's real autumn weather today.

work.title: Sharing unconfirmed news
work.description: Telling coworkers about something not yet official.
work.example: Apparently we're switching to a new system next month.

work.title: Complimenting a coworker
work.description: Praising someone's work as very much their style.
work.example: So careful down to the last detail. That's Tanaka-san for you.

etymology: There are several theories about the origin of らしい. It is generally thought to be related to the old suffix 「〜らし」, meaning "appearance, being like" (as in 「男らし」), and to have gradually developed its use as an auxiliary of inference from the medieval to the early modern period. Classical Japanese also had a separate conjectural auxiliary 「らし」 (expressing an inference based on evidence), but scholars disagree on whether there is a direct line of descent between the two.

similar.title: 〜ようだ／〜みたいだ
similar.explanation: 〜ようだ is based on the speaker's own observations and feelings, so the judgment is more subjective; 〜らしい is mostly based on outside information and has a "secondhand" feel. 「熱があるようだ」 (I feel I have a fever), 「熱があるらしい」 (I hear they have a fever).

similar.title: 〜そうだ (hearsay)
similar.explanation: The hearsay 〜そうだ is a faithful report with a clear source; 〜らしい mixes in inference, so its reliability is vaguer.

similar.title: 〜っぽい
similar.explanation: 「子どもっぽい」 means "childish (though not actually a child)", often negative; 「子どもらしい」 means "as a child should be", mostly positive.

meaning: A guess based on your own observation (“it seems ...”). It also makes comparisons (“like ...”) and gives examples. 「みたいだ」 is the casual form.
connection: ようだ: plain form / na-adjective + な / noun + の + ようだ; みたいだ: plain form / na-adjective stem / noun + みたいだ

senses.label: Inference
senses.meaning: A guess based on what you yourself see or feel: “it seems ...”, “it looks like ...”. The basis is the speaker's direct observation.
senses.connection: Plain form + ようだ／みたいだ (noun: 学生のようだ／学生みたいだ)
examples: It seems no one is here. The lights are off.
I feel like I've met that person somewhere.
I think I've caught a cold.

senses.label: Comparison
senses.meaning: Compares one thing to another: “like ...”, “as ... as ...”. Often paired with 「まるで」.
senses.connection: Noun + の + ようだ／ような／ように; noun + みたいだ／みたいな／みたいに
examples: Her hands were as cold as ice.
That sounds just like a dream.

senses.label: Giving examples
senses.meaning: Gives a concrete example: “such as ...”, “like ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + の + ような + noun; noun + みたいな + noun
examples: I want to live in a big city like Tokyo.
I like fruits like apples.

notes: 「ようだ」 is more formal and written; 「みたいだ」 is conversational and not suited to formal writing.
They attach differently: 静かなようだ ↔ 静かみたいだ; 学生のようだ ↔ 学生みたいだ.
「ようになる」, 「ようにする」, and 「〜ように」 (purpose) are separate grammar points.

daily.title: Noticing things at home
daily.description: Coming home and guessing that no one's back yet.
daily.example: Looks like nobody's home yet.

daily.title: Describing a beautiful view
daily.description: An exclamation at stunning scenery.
daily.example: The scenery is just like a painting.

daily.title: Feeling unwell
daily.description: Telling family how you feel.
daily.example: I think I have a bit of a fever.

work.title: Reporting an observation
work.description: Giving your boss your read on a situation, with polite 「ようです」.
work.example: It appears there's a problem with the system.

work.title: Explaining with an example
work.description: Showing in a meeting what kind of thing you want.
work.example: Could you prepare materials like this?

etymology: 「よう」 is the kanji 「様」, meaning "appearance, state", and with the copula だ it means "it is the appearance of ...". 「みたい」 developed through contraction from 「〜を見たような」 → 「〜みたような」 → 「みたい」, and is generally thought to have settled in colloquial speech after the Meiji era; that is why it still attaches directly to nouns.

similar.title: 〜らしい
similar.explanation: 〜ようだ is based on the speaker's own observations, 〜らしい on outside information. Similes can only use 〜ようだ／みたいだ, not らしい (✕夢らしい話).

similar.title: 〜そうだ (appearance)
similar.explanation: The appearance 〜そうだ is an intuitive impression of what's in front of you; 〜ようだ is an overall judgment. 「おいしそうだ」 = it looks delicious; 「おいしいようだ」 = it seems to be delicious (e.g. judging from how everyone is enjoying it).

similar.title: 〜ように (purpose)
similar.explanation: In 「忘れないようにメモする」, ように expresses purpose and follows a verb; ように for similes is usually preceded by "noun + の".

meaning: A hypothetical condition: “if ..., then ...”. It stresses that the first part is the condition for the second. Also used in set phrases for general rules, advice, and regret.
connection: Verb conditional form + ば (書けば, 食べれば, すれば, 来れば); i-adjective → 〜ければ; na-adjective / noun → 〜なら(ば)

senses.label: Hypothetical condition
senses.meaning: “If A is true, then B is true.” The focus is on A as the required condition for B. A is usually a state or condition.
senses.connection: Verb conditional form + ば; i-adjective minus い + ければ; negative: 〜なければ
examples: If it's cheap, I'll buy it.
If you have time, let's go together.

senses.label: General rule
senses.meaning: Whenever A happens, B always follows. Common for natural laws, proverbs, and common sense.
senses.connection: Verb conditional form + ば + result in present tense
examples: When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.
Add 3 to 2 and you get 5.

senses.label: Advice: 「〜ばいい」
senses.meaning: 「〜ばいい」 means “you just need to ...” or “it's fine if you ...”. It gives advice or asks what to do.
senses.connection: Verb conditional form + ばいい (asking how: どうすればいいですか)
examples: If you don't understand, just ask the teacher.
What should I do?

senses.label: Regret: 「〜ばよかった」
senses.meaning: 「〜ばよかった」 means “I should have ...”. It expresses regret about something you didn't do.
senses.connection: Verb conditional form + ばよかった
examples: We should have left earlier.
I should have brought an umbrella.

notes: When both parts share a subject and the first is a volitional verb, the second usually can't be a command, request, or intention. Use 「〜たら」 instead.
「〜ば〜ほど」 means “the more ..., the more ...”: 練習すればするほど上手になる.
The 「ば」 in 「てばかり」, 「例えば」, and 「言葉」 is not this grammar point.

daily.title: Hesitating while shopping
daily.description: Deciding whether to buy based on price while out with a friend.
daily.example: If it were a bit cheaper, I'd buy it.

daily.title: Asking for directions
daily.description: Asking a passerby the way.
daily.example: How do I get to the station?

daily.title: Regret after the fact
daily.description: Frustrated after missing the train.
daily.example: I should have left home a little earlier.

work.title: Advising a junior
work.description: Telling a newcomer what to do if they run into trouble.
work.example: If you have any problems, feel free to come to me anytime.

work.title: Discussing conditions
work.description: Explaining a prerequisite for a plan in a meeting.
work.example: If the budget allows, we can start next month.

etymology: In Classical Japanese, "irrealis form + ば" expressed a hypothetical condition ("if ..."), while "realis form + ば" expressed a fixed condition ("because ..., since ..."). From the medieval period onward, realis + ば gradually took on the hypothetical meaning too, and the irrealis + ば use declined. So the modern "conditional (hypothetical) form" actually evolved from the classical "realis form" (已然形), which is why some grammar books still call it by that name.

similar.title: 〜たら
similar.explanation: 〜たら has the widest range: its second clause can be a command, request, or intention, and it can also describe established facts ("when I did ..., I found ..."). 〜ば focuses on the condition itself, has restrictions on the second clause, and is common in writing and proverbs.

similar.title: 〜なら
similar.explanation: 〜なら takes up the listener's topic or assumes the first clause as a premise to give advice (「京都に行くなら、新幹線が便利だ」), and the time order of the two clauses can be reversed; 〜ば requires the first clause to happen before the second.

similar.title: 〜と
similar.explanation: 〜と expresses inevitable or habitual results (「春になると暖かくなる」), and its second clause cannot be an intention or request; 〜ば can also express general rules but puts more emphasis on the condition.

meaning: The most versatile conditional. It covers hypotheticals (“if ...”), sure sequences (“when / after ...”), unexpected discoveries, and suggestions.
connection: Ta-form of verbs, adjectives, or nouns + ら (行ったら, 高かったら, 静かだったら, 雨だったら)

senses.label: Hypothetical condition
senses.meaning: “If ...” The main clause can be a command, request, intention, or invitation, so it is more flexible than 「〜ば」. Often paired with 「もし」.
senses.connection: Ta-form + ら; negative: 〜なかったら
examples: If it rains, the game will be canceled.
If they're cheap, I'd like to buy two.

senses.label: When / once ...
senses.meaning: The first event is sure to happen: “once A happens, do B”. It isn't really a hypothesis.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ら + next action (often a request or intention)
examples: Please call me when you get to the station.
When I get home, I'll do my homework right away.

senses.label: Discovery
senses.meaning: With a past-tense main clause, it shows something you unexpectedly found after doing A: “When I ..., I found ...”.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ら + past tense (〜ていた／〜だった)
examples: When I opened the window, it was snowing outside.
When I got home, I found my mother had come over.

senses.label: Suggestion
senses.meaning: 「〜たらどう(ですか)」 and 「〜たらいい」 make suggestions: “Why don't you ...?”, “You could just ...”.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + らどうですか／らいい
examples: If you're tired, why not take a short break?
You could just ask the teacher.

notes: It sounds more conversational than 「〜ば」. In formal settings, use 「〜ましたら」 (わかりましたら、お知らせください).
The 「たら／だら」 in words like 「だらけ」 and 「はたらく」 is not this grammar point.

daily.title: Meeting up with a friend
daily.description: Asking a friend to get in touch on arrival.
daily.example: Send me a LINE when you get there.

daily.title: Giving a friend advice
daily.description: A suggestion when a friend isn't feeling well.
daily.example: Why don't you go see a doctor?

daily.title: Telling about a surprise
daily.description: Telling family about something unexpected.
daily.example: When I opened my bag, my wallet wasn't there.

work.title: Assigning a task
work.description: Asking a team member to report when finished.
work.example: Let me know when you're done.

work.title: Formally inviting a client to get in touch
work.description: Using 「〜ましたら」 in an email for politeness.
work.example: If you have any questions, please contact us.

etymology: 〜たら comes from 「たら」, the irrealis form of the Classical Japanese perfective auxiliary 「たり」, plus the conjunctive particle 「ば」, i.e. 「〜たらば」, meaning "if ... has happened". Later ば dropped off, leaving only 〜たら. The written form 「〜たらば」 can still occasionally be seen today.

similar.title: 〜ば
similar.explanation: 〜ば focuses on the condition, and its second clause shouldn't be an intention or request (when the first clause has a volitional verb); 〜たら has almost no restrictions, can also express time sequence and unexpected discoveries, and is more colloquial.

similar.title: 〜なら
similar.explanation: 「東京へ行ったら、スカイツリーに登りたい」 is about after arriving in Tokyo; 「東京へ行くなら、新幹線がいい」 is advice before going. 〜なら allows the second action to happen before the first clause has taken place.

similar.title: 〜たあとで
similar.explanation: 〜たあとで only expresses simple time order; 〜たら includes the sense that the first clause is the trigger or condition.

meaning: Picks up what someone said or a topic and uses it as a premise for advice or a judgment (“if that's the case ...”). Also used to mark a topic and for general conditions.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + なら; na-adjective stem / noun + なら (also 「ならば」; casual 「のなら／んなら」)

senses.label: Advice based on what was said
senses.meaning: Takes what the other person said as a premise and gives advice or an opinion: “If you're going to ...”. This is the most typical use of 「なら」.
senses.connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + なら (often followed by 「〜がいい」 or 「〜たほうがいい」)
examples: If you're going to Kyoto, autumn is a great time.
If you're buying a computer, this store is cheap.

senses.label: Topic marker
senses.meaning: Noun + 「なら」 narrows the topic to a specific person or thing: “as for ...”, “if it's ... you want”. Often used to answer someone's question.
senses.connection: Noun + なら
examples: If you're looking for Tanaka-san, he's in the library.
If you want beer, there's some in the fridge.

senses.label: General condition
senses.meaning: Simply means “if ...”. 「ならば」 is used for formality or emphasis.
senses.connection: Plain form / noun / na-adjective stem + なら(ば)
examples: If you're going, I'll go too.
If that's true, it's a serious matter.

notes: The order of events can be reversed: 「旅行に行くなら、カメラを買ったほうがいい」 (buy the camera first, then travel). 「〜ば」 and 「〜たら」 can't do this.
In speech, 「〜のなら／〜んなら」 is common: 行くんなら、早く行こう.
The 「なら」 in 「さようなら」, 「ならない」, 「習う」, and 「並ぶ」 is not this grammar point.

daily.title: A friend wants to travel
daily.description: Recommending a place based on what your friend said.
daily.example: If you're going to a hot spring, I recommend Hakone.

daily.title: Family looking for something
daily.description: Answering a family member's question.
daily.example: The scissors? They're in the drawer.

daily.title: A friend wants to buy something
daily.description: Giving advice based on their plans.
daily.example: If you want something cheap, you're better off buying online.

work.title: A coworker looking for someone
work.description: Telling a coworker where the person is.
work.example: If you're looking for the manager, she's in the meeting room.

work.title: Advising a client
work.description: Recommending a plan based on the client's needs.
work.example: If you'll be using it with a large group, this plan is a better deal.

etymology: 「なら」 is the irrealis form of the Classical Japanese copula 「なり」; with the conjunctive particle 「ば」 it forms 「ならば」, meaning "if it is ...". In modern colloquial speech ば is often dropped, giving 〜なら.

similar.title: 〜たら
similar.explanation: 〜たら requires the first clause to be realized first; with 〜なら the second action can happen before the first clause is realized. 「お酒を飲んだら運転するな」 (Once you've had a drink, don't drive), 「お酒を飲むなら運転するな」 (If you're going to drink, don't drive).

similar.title: 〜ば
similar.explanation: 〜ば stresses the relationship between condition and result; 〜なら stresses advice and judgments "premised on what the other person said".

similar.title: 〜のなら／〜んなら
similar.explanation: Adding の puts more emphasis on "given that this is the situation", making the link to the previous statement clearer; very common in speech.

meaning: The passive voice: the subject receives someone else's action (“be ...ed”), or is troubled by someone's action. Also used for objective descriptions.
connection: Godan: change the ending to the あ-row + れる (書かれる, 言われる); ichidan: drop る + られる (食べられる); する→される; 来る→来られる

senses.label: Direct passive
senses.meaning: The subject directly receives someone else's action: “be ...ed (by ...)”. The doer is marked with 「に」.
senses.connection: Doer に + verb passive form (叱られる, ほめられる, 呼ばれる)
examples: When I was a child, I often got scolded by my mother.
I was happy to be praised by my teacher.

senses.label: Possessor passive
senses.meaning: Your body part or belonging is affected by someone else's action. The person is the subject, and the affected part or item takes 「を」.
senses.connection: Person が／は + doer に + thing を + passive form
examples: Someone stepped on my foot on the train.
My wallet was stolen by a thief.

senses.label: Suffering passive
senses.meaning: You are troubled by someone's action or by nature. Intransitive verbs can be used too. In English it's often best expressed as something happening “on” you, as in “it rained on me”.
senses.connection: Doer に + intransitive / transitive verb passive form (雨に降られる, 子どもに泣かれる)
examples: I got caught in the rain on the way home and got soaked.
The baby kept crying in the middle of the night, so I couldn't sleep.

senses.label: Objective description
senses.meaning: With a thing as the subject, it states facts objectively. Common in news and explanatory writing. The doer is often omitted, or a creator is marked with 「によって」.
senses.connection: Thing は／が + passive form (〜によって 〜られる)
examples: This temple was built 500 years ago.
Japanese is studied all over the world.
This painting was painted by Picasso.

notes: For ichidan verbs and 「来る」, the passive looks the same as the potential and honorific forms (食べられる = be eaten / can eat / eat [honorific]). Context decides.
「生まれる」, 「疲れる」, 「別れる」, and 「慣れる」 are independent verbs, not passives.

daily.title: Complaining to a friend
daily.description: Telling about a bad moment on the train.
daily.example: Someone stepped on my foot on a packed train, and it hurt.

daily.title: Getting praised
daily.description: Sharing good news with family at home.
daily.example: My teacher praised me today!

daily.title: Introducing a sightseeing spot
daily.description: A guide explains a building's history.
daily.example: This castle was built 400 years ago.

work.title: Objective statements in news and reports
work.description: Stating facts objectively in a report.
work.example: The new product is scheduled to be released next month.

work.title: Explaining an assigned task
work.description: Telling a coworker the work came from the boss.
work.example: The department manager asked me to take on a new job.

etymology: The passive auxiliaries れる／られる come from Classical Japanese 「る／らる」. 「る・らる」 had four uses — spontaneous, potential, passive, and honorific — and their original core meaning is generally thought to have been "spontaneous" (something happening by itself), from which the other uses derived. This is the historical reason why the passive, potential, and honorific forms look the same in modern Japanese.

similar.title: 〜せる・〜させる (causative)
similar.explanation: The causative means "make / let someone do"; the passive means "have something done to you". The two combine in the causative-passive 〜させられる, meaning "be made to do" (「母に野菜を食べさせられた」).

similar.title: Potential form 〜られる
similar.explanation: For ichidan verbs the potential and passive forms are identical: 「この魚は生で食べられる」 (can be eaten) vs. 「魚が猫に食べられた」 (was eaten). The godan potential is 書ける, 読める, different from the passive 書かれる, 読まれる; the colloquial "ra-less" forms (見れる, 来れる) are potential only.

similar.title: Honorific 〜れる・〜られる
similar.explanation: In 「先生が来られました」, られる is honorific (the teacher came), not passive. Check whether the subject is someone to be respected and whether there is an agent marked with 「に」.

meaning: The causative voice: making or letting someone do something (by force or by permission). It can also mean causing someone to feel an emotion.
connection: Godan: change the ending to the あ-row + せる (行かせる, 読ませる); ichidan: drop る + させる (食べさせる); する→させる; 来る→来させる

senses.label: Making someone do
senses.meaning: Someone in a higher position makes someone do something: “make (someone) do ...”. With transitive verbs, the person made to act takes 「に」. With intransitive verbs, 「を」 is common.
senses.connection: Person に + object を + causative form; person を + intransitive causative form
examples: The mother makes her child eat vegetables every day.
The teacher had the students write an essay.

senses.label: Letting someone do
senses.meaning: Allowing someone to do what they want, or leaving them free to: “let (someone) ...”. Often 「〜させてあげる」.
senses.connection: Causative form + てあげる／てやる／ておく
examples: I let the kids play freely in the park.
My daughter said she wanted to study abroad, so I let her go.

senses.label: Please let me ...
senses.meaning: 「〜させてください」 asks permission to do something yourself: “Please let me ...”. More polite: 「〜させていただけませんか」.
senses.connection: Causative te-form + ください／いただけませんか
examples: Excuse me, please let me rest for a bit.
Please let me handle that job.

senses.label: Causing emotions
senses.meaning: Making someone feel something or react: “make (someone) happy / worried / wait”.
senses.connection: Person を + causative of an emotion verb (心配させる, 笑わせる, 待たせる)
examples: His jokes always make everyone laugh.
Sorry to keep you waiting so long.

notes: The causative-passive 「〜させられる」 means “be made to do”: 母に野菜を食べさせられた. For godan verbs, speech often shortens it to 「行かされる」 or 「待たされる」.
Avoid using the causative directly toward superiors; it can sound rude.

daily.title: Parents setting rules
daily.description: Explaining a household rule.
daily.example: Every night, I make my kids brush their teeth.

daily.title: Apologizing for being late
daily.description: Saying sorry for keeping a friend waiting.
daily.example: Sorry I kept you waiting!

daily.title: Letting a child do what they love
daily.description: A parent lets their child learn something they enjoy.
daily.example: My son loves soccer, so we've signed him up for lessons.

work.title: Asking your boss
work.description: Politely asking permission with 「〜させていただけませんか」.
work.example: Would it be possible for me to take tomorrow off?

work.title: Volunteering for a task
work.description: Offering to take something on in a meeting.
work.example: Please let me take charge of that matter.

etymology: The causative auxiliaries せる／させる come from Classical Japanese 「す／さす」 (there was also 「しむ」). 「す」 attached to the irrealis form of yodan verbs and 「さす」 to other verbs, corresponding one-to-one with modern godan + せる and ichidan + させる. From the medieval period on, both shifted to shimo-ichidan conjugation and became 「せる・させる」. Classical 「す・さす」 also had an honorific use (as in 「せさせ給ふ」), which has disappeared in modern Japanese.

similar.title: 〜れる・〜られる (passive)
similar.explanation: The passive means "be ...ed"; the causative means "make / let ...". The causative-passive 〜させられる means "be forced to ...", with a sense of reluctance.

similar.title: 〜てもらう
similar.explanation: 〜てもらう means "have someone do something for you", with gratitude and a sense of a favor (「友だちに手伝ってもらった」); the causative is a command or permission from above, with no sense of a favor.

similar.title: Transitive verbs
similar.explanation: Some transitive/intransitive verb pairs are close in meaning to the causative: 「子どもを起こす」 (wake the child up, transitive) vs. 「子どもを起きさせる」 (make the child get up by themselves). The transitive verb means acting directly; the causative means having the other person do it themselves.

meaning: The speaker (or their side) does something for someone else as a favor. Use 「てさしあげる」 toward superiors and 「てやる」 toward juniors, animals, and plants.
connection: Verb te-form + あげる (humble: 〜てさしあげる; downward: 〜てやる)

senses.label: Doing for others
senses.meaning: The giver (usually your side) does something for someone else: “do ... for someone”. The receiver is marked with 「に」 or 「の」.
senses.connection: Person に／person の + thing を + verb te-form + あげる
examples: I read a book to my little sister.
I showed a lost person the way to the station.
That looks heavy. Let me carry it for you.

senses.label: For superiors (humble)
senses.meaning: 「〜てさしあげる」 is the humble form for elders and superiors. Even so, saying it to their face sounds like you're doing them a favor, so 「お〜します」 is usually used instead.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + さしあげる
examples: I carried my teacher's bag for her.

senses.label: For juniors and animals
senses.meaning: 「〜てやる」 is for doing things for juniors, animals, or plants. It can also mean “I'll show you!” in a defiant tone.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + やる
examples: Every morning, I take the dog out for a walk.
I fixed my little brother's bike for him.
This time I'm definitely going to win.

notes: Saying 「〜てあげましょうか」 directly to a superior sounds condescending. The polite way is 「お持ちしましょうか」.
It can't be used when the speaker receives the favor. Use 「〜てくれる」 instead.

daily.title: Looking after younger siblings
daily.description: Telling a friend how you helped your brother.
daily.example: I helped my little brother with his homework.

daily.title: Helping a friend
daily.description: Offering to help when a friend is carrying something heavy.
daily.example: I'll carry that bag for you.

daily.title: Taking care of a pet
daily.description: Explaining your daily pet care.
daily.example: Making breakfast for the cat is my job every morning.

work.title: Mentoring a junior
work.description: Telling a coworker how you helped a new hire.
work.example: I showed the new hire how to do the job.

work.title: Avoid with superiors
work.description: Don't say 「〜てあげましょうか」 to a superior. Use the humble 「お〜します」 instead.
work.example: Shall I carry the documents for you, sir? (not ✕持ってあげましょうか)

etymology: あげる is written 「上げる」, originally meaning "to raise, to lift up". Lifting something up to offer it to a person of higher status gave rise to the meaning "to give". It was originally a humble word but gradually became neutral, meaning ordinary "give", so its original humble role was taken over by さしあげる (差し上げる).

similar.title: 〜てくれる
similar.explanation: 〜てくれる means someone else does something for "me (or my side)"; 〜てあげる means I do something for someone else. The directions are opposite.

similar.title: 〜てもらう
similar.explanation: 〜てもらう takes the recipient as subject: "I have / get someone to do it for me"; 〜てあげる takes the giver as subject.

similar.title: お〜する
similar.explanation: When offering help to an elder, the humble 「お持ちしましょうか」 is more appropriate than 「持ってあげましょうか」.

meaning: Someone does something for the speaker (or their side), and the speaker is grateful. Use 「てくださる」 for superiors.
connection: Verb te-form + くれる (honorific: 〜てくださる)

senses.label: Someone does it for me
senses.meaning: The giver is the subject, and the receiver is “me” or my side. 「私に」 is usually left out. It conveys gratitude.
senses.connection: Person が + verb te-form + くれる／くれた
examples: My friends helped me move.
Thank you for coming.
My mom always listens to me.

senses.label: A superior does it for me
senses.meaning: 「〜てくださる」 is the honorific form, for when an elder or superior does something for you. Its masu-form is 「くださいます」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + くださる／くださいます／くださった
examples: My teacher corrected my essay for me.
The company president drove me to the station.

senses.label: Requests
senses.meaning: 「〜てくれない？」 and 「〜てくれませんか」 ask someone for help, more softly than 「〜てください」. 「〜てくれ」 is a blunt order used by men toward equals or juniors.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + くれない？／くれませんか／くれ
examples: Could you pass me the salt?
Excuse me, could you open the door for me?

notes: It can't be used when the receiver isn't on your side: ✕「田中さんが山田さんに教えてくれた」. Between outsiders, use 「〜てあげた」.
「〜てください」 is a request form and isn't the 「てくださる」 covered here.

daily.title: Thanking a friend
daily.description: Thanking a friend for making the effort to visit.
daily.example: Thanks for coming all this way.

daily.title: Asking family for help at the table
daily.description: Casually asking someone to pass something.
daily.example: Can you pass the soy sauce?

daily.title: Talking about family help
daily.description: Telling a friend about a parent's support.
daily.example: My dad gave me a ride to the station.

work.title: Thanking your boss
work.description: Showing gratitude for guidance with the honorific form.
work.example: The department manager took the time to teach me carefully.

work.title: Asking a coworker for help
work.description: A small favor asked in a soft tone.
work.example: Could you make a copy of this for me?

etymology: くれる is written 「呉れる」; the old verb 「くる（呉る）」 meant "to give (to an inferior, to oneself)". From the medieval period on it was used specifically in the direction "someone gives to me", forming, together with あげる and もらう, Japanese's distinctive system of giving and receiving verbs. くださる is written 「下さる」, originally "to bestow (from above)", hence its honorific nature.

similar.title: 〜てあげる
similar.explanation: Opposite direction: 〜てあげる means I do something for others; 〜てくれる means others do something for me.

similar.title: 〜てもらう
similar.explanation: 「友だちが手伝ってくれた」 and 「友だちに手伝ってもらった」 describe the same fact; the former takes the giver as subject, the latter the recipient, and 〜てもらう can also imply "I asked for it".

similar.title: 〜てください
similar.explanation: 〜てください is a direct request; 〜てくれませんか／〜てくださいませんか are requests in question form, softer and more polite.

meaning: You have someone do something for you, or you benefit from someone's action. Use 「ていただく」 for superiors.
connection: Verb te-form + もらう (humble: 〜ていただく)

senses.label: Having someone do it for me
senses.meaning: The receiver (usually me) is the subject, and the giver is marked with 「に」. It can mean you asked for it or simply that you benefited: “have / get someone to ...”.
senses.connection: Person に + verb te-form + もらう; for superiors: 〜ていただく
examples: I had my friends help me move.
I had a doctor examine me at the hospital.
My teacher kindly corrected my essay.

senses.label: Polite requests
senses.meaning: 「〜てもらえませんか」 and 「〜ていただけませんか」 are very polite, very common request forms: “Could you possibly ...?”.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + もらえませんか／いただけませんか
examples: Excuse me, could you take a picture for me?
Could you explain it once more, please?

senses.label: Wanting someone to do
senses.meaning: 「〜てもらいたい」 and 「〜ていただきたい」 express wanting someone to do something. More formal than 「〜てほしい」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + もらいたい／いただきたい
examples: I'd really like you to read this book.
We'd like all of you to take part as well.

notes: The giver can also be marked with 「から」: 先生から教えてもらった.
「もらう」 alone (receiving an item) and 「いただきます」 (said before eating) are not this grammar point.

daily.title: Asking someone to take a photo
daily.description: Politely asking a passerby at a tourist spot.
daily.example: Excuse me, could you take a picture for us?

daily.title: Talking about a friend's help
daily.description: Telling family how a friend helped.
daily.example: A friend gave me a ride to the station.

daily.title: At the hair salon
daily.description: Saying you got your hair cut.
daily.example: I got my hair cut yesterday.

work.title: Asking your boss to review something
work.description: Politely asking a superior to check materials.
work.example: Could you take a look at these materials?

work.title: Assigning a task to a junior
work.description: Saying what you want them to do.
work.example: I'd like you to have this summarized by tomorrow.

etymology: もらう is written 「貰う」, originally meaning "to ask for and receive". いただく is written 「頂く／戴く」, originally "to place on top of one's head" — when receiving something from a person of higher status, one raised it above one's head out of respect — and so it became the humble word for "to receive" (the 「いただきます」 said before meals comes from this too).

similar.title: 〜てくれる
similar.explanation: For the same event, 〜てくれる takes the giver as subject and stresses that they did it for me of their own accord; 〜てもらう takes me as subject and can imply "I asked for it".

similar.title: 〜てあげる
similar.explanation: 〜てあげる means I do something for others; the direction of the favor is opposite to 〜てもらう.

similar.title: Causative 〜させる
similar.explanation: The causative is a command or permission from above; 〜てもらう is a request with gratitude toward the other person. 「子どもに掃除させる」 (make the child clean) and 「子どもに掃除してもらう」 (have the child kindly clean) differ greatly in tone.

meaning: Contrast: the result goes against expectations, with a tone of dissatisfaction, regret, or surprise (“even though ...”). At the end of a sentence, it expresses regret.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + のに; na-adjective / noun + なのに

senses.label: Even though ...
senses.meaning: The result is the opposite of what the first part leads you to expect. It carries dissatisfaction, regret, or blame. The second part is something that has happened or is certain.
senses.connection: Plain form + のに; noun / na-adjective + なのに (✕日曜日だのに)
examples: We'd made plans, but he never showed up.
Even though it's Sunday, I have to go to the office.
It's already April, and it's still cold.

senses.label: Regret at the end
senses.meaning: At the end of a sentence, it expresses regret or frustration that things didn't go as hoped: “If only ...”, “I wish ...”. Often 「〜ばいいのに」 or 「〜ばよかったのに」.
senses.connection: 〜ば + いいのに／よかったのに; plain form + のに (sentence-final)
examples: You should have told me.
If only you lived a bit closer.
And I went to all the trouble of making it...

notes: The second part can't be a command, request, or intention: ✕「雨なのに、出かけてください」. Use 「〜けど」 or 「〜ても」 instead.
Purpose 「〜のに」 (物を入れるのに便利だ) has a different meaning and isn't covered here.

daily.title: Upset with a friend
daily.description: Complaining when a friend didn't keep their word.
daily.example: I was waiting for you. Why didn't you come?

daily.title: Complaining about the weather
daily.description: When the weather doesn't match the season.
daily.example: It's already spring, and it's snowing.

daily.title: Feeling sorry for someone
daily.description: When a friend missed out on something good.
daily.example: You should have come too.

work.title: Disappointed with a result
work.description: Telling a coworker your efforts didn't pay off.
work.example: We prepared so much, but we didn't win the contract.

work.title: Watching your tone at work
work.description: 「のに」 sounds accusing. When explaining to a boss or client, use 「〜が」 instead.
work.example: I did get in touch, but I didn't receive a reply. (not ✕連絡したのに)

etymology: Made of the formal noun / nominalizing particle 「の」 + the case particle 「に」, originally meaning "in the situation of ...". From the early modern period onward it became fixed as a contrastive conjunctive particle expressing a result contrary to expectation and the speaker's dissatisfaction.

similar.title: 〜けれども／〜が
similar.explanation: 〜けど／〜が are neutral contrasts that just state the two clauses differ; 〜のに carries strong emotions such as dissatisfaction or surprise, and its second clause cannot be a request or intention.

similar.title: 〜にもかかわらず
similar.explanation: Close in meaning to 〜のに, but written, more objective, and without strong personal emotion; common in news and essays.

similar.title: 〜ので
similar.explanation: 〜ので expresses a cause ("because ..., so"); 〜のに expresses contrast ("even though ..."). Be careful not to confuse them.

meaning: Lists parallel facts or reasons (“... and ..., and ...”), or gives one or two reasons while implying there are more.
connection: Plain form + し (noun / na-adjective: 〜だし); also after polite forms: 〜ですし／〜ますし

senses.label: Listing
senses.meaning: Lists several facts or features pointing the same way (all good or all bad): “not only ... but also ...”. Often paired with 「も」.
senses.connection: Aし、Bし、(それに) C; often 「〜も〜し、〜も〜」
examples: This apartment is spacious and close to the station, so it's really convenient.
He's kind, and he's a good cook too.
He's smart, and he has a great personality.

senses.label: Giving reasons
senses.meaning: Gives one or two reasons, implies there are others, then leads to a conclusion. It sounds softer than 「から」 and doesn't pin everything on one reason.
senses.connection: Reason + し、(reason + し、) + conclusion
examples: It's raining and it's cold today, so I don't want to go out.
We're short on time, so let's take a taxi.

senses.label: Sentence-final excuse
senses.meaning: At the end of a sentence, it states only the reason and leaves the conclusion for the listener to infer, like “... you know”. Often used in speech to make excuses softly.
senses.connection: Plain form + し。(often with 「だって」)
examples: Well, it's raining.
It's fine. I'm free anyway.

notes: Nouns and na-adjectives need 「だ」: 静かだし, 雨だし.
The 「し」 in 「ただし」 and 「わたし」 is not this grammar point.

daily.title: Recommending a restaurant
daily.description: Listing a place's good points for a friend.
daily.example: That place is cheap and tasty. I recommend it.

daily.title: Turning down an invitation
daily.description: Listing reasons to decline gently.
daily.example: I'm tired today, and I have an early start tomorrow, so I'm heading home.

daily.title: A sentence-final excuse
daily.description: Giving a reason when asked why you didn't do something.
daily.example: Well, it's such a hassle.

work.title: Making a suggestion in a meeting
work.description: Listing reasons to support a proposal, using polite 「ですし」.
work.example: It's cheap and it doesn't take much time, so I think this method is best.

work.title: Evaluating a new hire
work.description: Listing a new employee's strengths to your boss.
work.example: He works fast, and he's conscientious.

etymology: The conjunctive particle 「し」 is generally thought to derive from 「し」, the attributive form of the Classical Japanese past auxiliary 「き」, or from the emphatic adverbial particle 「し」; from the early modern period it developed into a conjunctive particle for listing parallel items and reasons. There are several theories about its origin, and none is settled.

similar.title: 〜から
similar.explanation: 〜から clearly states one reason; 〜し lists several reasons, or gives one while implying others, and sounds softer.

similar.title: 〜たり〜たりする
similar.explanation: 〜たり〜たり lists actions (as examples); 〜し lists facts, qualities, or reasons.

similar.title: 〜て／〜くて
similar.explanation: 「安くておいしい」 simply joins two qualities; 「安いし、おいしい」 stresses that "there's more than one reason" and often carries a judgment or evaluation.

meaning: Something goes beyond the proper limit: “too ...”, “over-...”. Usually negative.
connection: Verb masu-stem + すぎる; i-adjective minus い + すぎる (いい→よすぎる, ない→なさすぎる); na-adjective stem + すぎる

senses.label: Doing too much
senses.meaning: With verbs, it means overdoing an action: “too much”, “over-...”.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + すぎる (食べすぎる, 飲みすぎる, 働きすぎる)
examples: I ate too much cake yesterday.
Please don't drink too much.

senses.label: Too ...
senses.meaning: With adjectives, a quality goes beyond what is appropriate: “too ...”, “overly ...”.
senses.connection: i-adjective minus い / na-adjective stem + すぎる
examples: This bag is too expensive for me to buy.
This room is too quiet. It feels a bit lonely.
Having too little confidence isn't good either.

senses.label: Noun 「〜すぎ」
senses.meaning: As the noun 「〜すぎ」, it refers to the excess itself. Very common in speech.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem / adjective stem + すぎ(だ／に)
examples: That's going a bit too far.
Be careful not to overeat.

notes: It's usually negative, but in casual speech it's also used for exaggerated praise: かわいすぎる！おいしすぎる！
「10時過ぎ」 (past ten o'clock), 「時間が過ぎる」 (time passes), and 「〜にすぎない」 are not this grammar point.

daily.title: After a big meal
daily.description: Feeling uncomfortable from eating too much.
daily.example: I'm stuffed. I ate too much.

daily.title: Shopping
daily.description: Deciding something is too pricey to buy.
daily.example: This coat is a bit too expensive.

daily.title: Over-the-top praise
daily.description: Reacting to a cute little animal.
daily.example: This kitten is way too cute!

work.title: Worrying about an overworked coworker
work.description: Telling a coworker not to wear themselves out.
work.example: Haven't you been working too hard lately? Take a little break.

work.title: Evaluating a plan
work.description: Pointing out a problem with the plan.
work.example: I think this schedule is too tight.

etymology: すぎる is written with the kanji meaning "pass", and originally meant "to pass by, to go through (a place or time)". Going past a certain point means "exceeding" it, which extended to "going beyond the limit" in degree. In Classical Japanese it was the kami-nidan verb すぐ, which later became the kami-ichidan すぎる. (English "overdo" and "go too far" follow a similar logic.)

similar.title: あまり〜ない
similar.explanation: 「あまり高くない」 means "not very expensive"; 「高すぎる」 means "too expensive (beyond what's acceptable)". The former is a low degree, the latter an excessive one.

similar.title: とても／すごく
similar.explanation: 「とても高い」 just means very expensive, not necessarily a problem; 「高すぎる」 clearly means it exceeds the limit and causes a problem.

similar.title: 〜にすぎない
similar.explanation: The N2 「〜にすぎない」 means "is nothing more than ...". Although it also uses すぎ, it expresses a low, negligible degree — the exact opposite of "excess".

meaning: Something is easy or convenient to do, or something tends to happen: “easy to ...”, “prone to ...”.
connection: Verb masu-stem + やすい

senses.label: Easy to do
senses.meaning: An action is easy or convenient to do. Usually positive: “easy to ...”.
senses.connection: Volitional verb masu-stem + やすい (読みやすい, 使いやすい, わかりやすい)
examples: This pen is really easy to write with.
The teacher's explanation was easy to understand.
I want a computer that's easy to use.

senses.label: Prone to happen
senses.meaning: Something tends to change or happen easily. Usually with non-volitional verbs, and often negative: “prone to ...”, “tends to ...”.
senses.connection: Non-volitional verb masu-stem + やすい (割れやすい, 風邪をひきやすい)
examples: It's easy to catch a cold in winter, so please take care.
This glass breaks easily.

notes: It conjugates like an i-adjective: やすかった, やすくない, やすくなる.
It sounds the same as 「安い」 (cheap), but the meaning is different.
The opposite is 「〜にくい」. In writing, “prone to (bad things)” can also be 「〜がちだ」.

daily.title: Choosing a product
daily.description: Comparing items in a shop.
daily.example: This bag is light and easy to carry.

daily.title: Talking about health
daily.description: Saying you get sick easily when seasons change.
daily.example: It's easy to get run down when the seasons change.

daily.title: Recommending a study book
daily.description: Telling a friend about an easy-to-follow book.
daily.example: This book is really easy to understand.

work.title: Improving materials
work.description: A boss asks for clearer documents.
work.example: Please make the materials a little easier to read.

work.title: Describing the workplace
work.description: Telling a coworker about the new office.
work.example: The new office is spacious and easy to work in.

etymology: やすい is written 「易い」 and shares its origin with 「安い」; the old word 「やすし」 originally meant "calm, carefree, at ease". From "feeling at ease" it extended to "easy to do", and it became the second element of compound adjectives after the verb continuative form.

similar.title: 〜にくい
similar.explanation: Opposite: 〜にくい means "hard to ..., not easy to ...". 「読みやすい」 ↔ 「読みにくい」.

similar.title: 〜がちだ
similar.explanation: 〜がち means "tends to (often, something bad)", stressing frequency and tendency; 〜やすい stresses the quality of being "prone to". 「病気がちだ」 = often sick; 「病気になりやすい」 = easily gets sick.

similar.title: 〜やすい／安い
similar.explanation: 「安い（やすい）」 means "cheap" and is used as a standalone adjective; the やすい in this grammar point must follow a verb masu-stem.

meaning: Something is hard or awkward to do, or doesn't easily happen: “hard to ...”, “not easily ...”.
connection: Verb masu-stem + にくい

senses.label: Hard to do
senses.meaning: An action is difficult or inconvenient to do: “hard to ...”.
senses.connection: Volitional verb masu-stem + にくい (読みにくい, 歩きにくい, 使いにくい)
examples: This writing is so small it's hard to read.
My new shoes were still hard to walk in.

senses.label: Awkward to say or ask
senses.meaning: Hesitating to do something out of consideration for others: “it's awkward to ...”, “hard to bring up”.
senses.connection: Masu-stem of 「言う」, 「聞く」, 「頼む」, etc. + にくい
examples: There are some things I feel awkward asking my teacher.
He looks busy, so it's hard to ask him.

senses.label: Doesn't easily happen
senses.meaning: Something doesn't change or happen easily. Here it's usually positive and often describes product features.
senses.connection: Non-volitional verb masu-stem + にくい (割れにくい, 燃えにくい, 汚れにくい)
examples: This glass doesn't break easily.
These clothes are made of a stain-resistant material.

notes: It conjugates like an i-adjective: にくかった, にくくない, にくくなる.
The similar 「〜づらい」 focuses on the action being painful or uncomfortable and is more conversational.
「憎い」 (hateful) and 「肉」 (meat, as in とりにく) are not this grammar point.

daily.title: Food that's hard to eat
daily.description: Explaining why something is awkward to eat.
daily.example: This fish has so many bones, it's hard to eat.

daily.title: Opening up to a friend
daily.description: Bringing up something you feel awkward saying.
daily.example: It's kind of hard to tell my parents, but...

daily.title: Choosing a product
daily.description: A clerk points out a product's strengths.
daily.example: This frying pan doesn't burn food easily.

work.title: Raising a difficult issue
work.description: Gently telling your boss something hard to say.
work.example: I'm sorry to have to say this, but it doesn't look like we'll make the deadline.

work.title: Giving feedback on a system
work.description: Telling the person in charge the system is clunky.
work.example: This system is a bit hard to use.

etymology: にくい is written 「憎い／難い」; the old word 「にくし」 originally meant "hateful, detestable". From "hateful to do" it extended to "hard to do", and as the second element of compound adjectives after the verb continuative form it expresses difficulty. Used on its own, 「憎い」 still keeps the meaning "hateful".

similar.title: 〜やすい
similar.explanation: Opposite: 〜やすい "easy to ...". 「わかりやすい」 ↔ 「わかりにくい」.

similar.title: 〜づらい
similar.explanation: 〜づらい stresses that doing it is painful or uncomfortable (「足が痛くて歩きづらい」) and is mostly used for people's subjective feelings; for qualities of objects like 「割れにくい」, 割れづらい is generally not used.

similar.title: 〜かねる
similar.explanation: 〜かねる (N2) means "(given one's position) cannot ...", a formal and polite way of declining (「お答えしかねます」); different from 〜にくい, which is about objective difficulty.

meaning: The speaker's intention or plan: “I think I'll ...”, “I'm going to ...”. 「〜ようと思っている」 is a plan held for some time.
connection: Verb volitional form + と思う (行こう, 食べよう, しよう, 来よう)

senses.label: A decision now
senses.meaning: 「〜(よ)うと思う」 is a decision or idea made at the moment of speaking. The subject is first person: “I think I'll ...”.
senses.connection: Verb volitional form + と思う／と思います
examples: I think I'll go see a movie with friends this weekend.
I think I'll go to bed early tonight.

senses.label: A plan held for a while
senses.meaning: 「〜(よ)うと思っている」 is a plan you've had for some time. It can also be used for a third person.
senses.connection: Verb volitional form + と思っている／と思っています
examples: I'm planning to study abroad in Japan next year.
My brother has been thinking of buying a car.

senses.label: Meant to, but didn't
