senses.meaning: 「〜(よ)うと思った」 often means you had the idea at the time but didn't end up doing it. Often followed by 「けど」 or 「のに」.
senses.connection: Verb volitional form + と思った(けど／が)
examples: I meant to call yesterday, but I forgot.
Just as I was about to go out, it started raining.

notes: Volitional form: godan verbs change the ending to the お-row + う (書こう, 読もう, 買おう); ichidan verbs drop る + よう; する→しよう; 来る→来よう.
For a more formal, well-considered plan, say 「〜(よ)うと考えている」.
Plain form + 「と思う」 (来ると思う) is a guess, not this grammar point.

daily.title: Talking about weekend plans
daily.description: Answering when a friend asks about your weekend.
daily.example: I think I'll just relax at home this weekend.

daily.title: New Year's goals
daily.description: Announcing your resolution to family.
daily.example: This year I'm going to exercise every day.

daily.title: Explaining something you didn't do
daily.description: Telling a friend why you didn't get in touch.
daily.example: I meant to contact you, but I was so busy.

work.title: Career plans in an interview
work.description: Explaining your future plans in an interview.
work.example: In the future, I'm thinking of working overseas.

work.title: Reporting your plans to your boss
work.description: Explaining what you'll work on next.
work.example: I'm planning to put the materials together this afternoon.

etymology: The volitional 〜(よ)う comes from the Classical Japanese conjectural auxiliary 「む」 (→ん→う), which expressed intention and conjecture; 「よう」 is the form 「う」 took after ichidan verbs. Classical 「〜むと思ふ」 already meant "I intend to ...", and modern 〜(よ)うと思う directly inherits this structure.

similar.title: 〜つもりだ
similar.explanation: 〜つもりだ is a settled, fairly firm plan; 〜(よ)うと思う is often a fresh idea or a plan that may still change, and sounds softer.

similar.title: 〜たい
similar.explanation: 〜たい only expresses a wish and doesn't necessarily lead to action; 〜(よ)うと思う expresses an intention to do it.

similar.title: 〜ようとする
similar.explanation: 〜ようとする means "be about to, try to" do something (「出かけようとしたとき、電話が鳴った」); it describes the moment just before an action or an attempt, not an inner plan.

meaning: Shows what stage an action is at: about to start, in progress, or just finished. Also has related uses such as “almost ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / ている-form / ta-form + ところだ

senses.label: About to
senses.meaning: The action is about to start but hasn't yet: “just about to ...”. Often with 「今から」, 「これから」, or 「ちょうど」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ところだ
examples: I'm just about to head out.
I'm about to have dinner.

senses.label: In the middle of
senses.meaning: The action is in progress: “in the middle of ...”. It stresses being in the process right now more than 「〜ている」 does.
senses.connection: Verb ている-form + ところだ (often with 「今」)
examples: I'm making dinner right now.
We're looking into that matter now.

senses.label: Just finished
senses.meaning: The action has just ended: “have just ...”. Often with 「たった今」, 「今」, or 「ちょうど」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ところだ
examples: I just got to the station.
I've just finished work.

senses.label: Almost
senses.meaning: 「〜ところだった」 means something almost happened but didn't. Often paired with 「もう少しで」 or 「危うく」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ところだった
examples: I almost missed the train.
That was close. I nearly hit a car.

senses.label: Just when ...
senses.meaning: 「〜ところに／へ」 means something else happened at that moment (someone came, the phone rang, etc.). 「〜ところを」 means you were seen or interrupted in the middle of something.
senses.connection: Verb (various forms) + ところに／ところへ／ところを
examples: Just as I was about to go out, the phone rang.
My teacher saw me while I was smoking.
Sorry to bother you when you're so busy.

notes: 「ところ」 originally means “place”. Don't confuse it with noun uses like 「住むところ」 (a place to live).
「ところで」 means “by the way” and changes the topic. It isn't this grammar point.

daily.title: A friend calls
daily.description: Explaining what you're doing right now.
daily.example: Sorry, I'm in the middle of eating.

daily.title: Telling someone where you are
daily.description: Letting a waiting friend know you just arrived.
daily.example: I just got to the station.

daily.title: A close call
daily.description: Telling family about a near accident.
daily.example: I almost fell down the stairs today.

work.title: Updating your boss on progress
work.description: Saying the work is in progress.
work.example: I'm currently putting the materials together.

work.title: Apologizing for interrupting
work.description: Greeting someone who is busy.
work.example: I'm very sorry to trouble you when you're so busy.

etymology: 「ところ」 is written 「所」, originally meaning "place, location". From a "position" in space it extended to a "position, stage" in the progress of time, giving the uses "about to / in the middle of / just finished". As a formal noun it is usually written in kana. (Compare English "at this point" used for time.)

similar.title: 〜たばかり
similar.explanation: 〜たところ refers to the moment just after completion in actual time; 〜たばかり means the speaker feels "not long ago" and can be used even after several months (「先月来たばかりです」), whereas ✕先月来たところです.

similar.title: 〜ている
similar.explanation: 〜ている simply expresses an ongoing action; 〜ているところだ stresses "right in the middle of it at this very moment" and is often used to explain why you're busy now.

similar.title: 〜ようとする
similar.explanation: 〜ようとする means "try to, be about to", with a sense of intention; 〜るところだ objectively describes the stage in time.

meaning: Not much time has passed since an action was completed: “just ...”. It stresses that the speaker feels the time was short.
connection: Verb ta-form + ばかりだ (casual: 〜たばっかり)

senses.label: Just did
senses.meaning: Not long has passed since the action. How long depends on the speaker's feeling; even a month later, you can still say “I just ...”.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ばかりだ／ばかりです
examples: I just came to Japan last week.
I only just joined this company, so I don't know anything yet.

senses.label: Just ...ed (before a noun)
senses.meaning: 「〜たばかりの + noun」 describes a noun: “freshly ...ed”, “just ...ed”.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ばかりの + noun
examples: I lost the umbrella I had just bought.
Newborn babies are really tiny.

senses.label: Only just ..., and yet
senses.meaning: 「〜たばかりなのに」 means “even though I only just ...”, with surprise or frustration.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ばかりなのに
examples: I just ate, and I'm already hungry.
I just bought it, and it's already broken.

notes: 「〜たところだ」 stresses the objective moment something ended; 「〜たばかりだ」 stresses the subjective feeling that not much time has passed.
Don't confuse it with 「〜てばかりいる」 (“always doing ...”). That follows the te-form and means something completely different.

daily.title: Introducing yourself
daily.description: Introducing yourself somewhere new.
daily.example: I just moved to Tokyo.

daily.title: Complaining about something broken
daily.description: Grumbling to a friend about something new.
daily.example: I dropped my brand-new phone and cracked it.

daily.title: Declining food
daily.description: Telling a friend you just ate when they offer food.
daily.example: I just ate, so I'm good.

work.title: A new hire asking for guidance
work.description: Saying you've just joined and asking for help.
work.example: I've only just joined the company, so I'd appreciate any guidance.

work.title: Explaining a project has just started
work.description: Updating your boss on a project.
work.example: This project has only just started.

etymology: 「ばかり」 comes from 「はかり」, the noun form of the verb 「計る（はかる）」 (to measure), originally meaning "estimate, approximate extent"; it later became voiced as the adverbial particle 「ばかり」, meaning "about, only, just". 〜たばかり thus means "only (that little time) since doing it", hence "have just done".

similar.title: 〜たところだ
similar.explanation: 〜たところ is the moment right after something ends in actual time; 〜たばかり is "not long ago" in a psychological sense, can cover a longer span, and can modify nouns (「買ったばかりの本」), while 〜たところ can't modify nouns this way to mean "just ...ed".

similar.title: 〜たあとで
similar.explanation: 〜たあとで only expresses order and says nothing about how much time passed; 〜たばかり stresses "very recently".

similar.title: 〜てばかりいる
similar.explanation: 「遊んでばかりいる」 means "always playing, doing nothing but play"; it follows the te-form and has nothing to do with "just".
